column4: The section's source phrase “aḥkamu l-ḥākimīn” is spoken by Noah while pleading for his son, whom he calls family and ties to God's promise; the plea shows how trust in the best Judge meets a painful family case.
The section's “khayru l-ḥākimīn” refrain appears as Shuʿayb tells his people to wait until God judges between them; it gives the section's final question a voice of patience amid division.

The section names the same “khayru l-ḥākimīn” wording in the command to the Prophet to wait for God's judgment; this makes the final question a ground for patient trust, not only a claim about divine rank.
The section cites the brother who will remain in Egypt until his father permits him or God judges for him; the verse stages waiting in place for the very “khayru l-ḥākimīn” named in the image.

After Shuʿayb's people threaten to expel him and the believers, he asks God to “open/judge between us and our people with truth” (افتح بيننا وبين قومنا بالحق); this makes the section's ḥukm a resolution of threatened injustice.

The section cites Noah's appeal in 11:45 for his son as family; the next ayah answers that the son is not of his family in the relevant sense and warns Noah not to ask without knowledge, showing the limit that divine judgment sets on kinship.
After the correction in 11:46, Noah seeks refuge from asking what he does not know and asks for mercy; this next turn shows him accepting the Judge's correction.
This ayah joins the section's two distinct words: the dead are “returned” (رُدّوا) to their true Master, then “judgment” (الحكم) is declared His. The return of 95:5 and rule of 95:8 become one scene.
God says that the disputants return to Him and that He will judge between them over what they differed about; it puts the section's return and judgment together on the resurrection horizon.

The command “refer it back to God and the Messenger” (فردّوه إلى الله والرسول) sends disputes to divine judgment. The ayah's radd is a different root from the section's dictionary form aḥkamtu (“I returned him”), but makes the same movement toward adjudication.
The section glosses calling someone to God's ruling; here whatever people dispute “its judgment belongs to God” (فحكمه إلى الله), directly naming that recourse.
The section calls dīn the day of judgment and cites the root q-w-m behind resurrection; this ayah says God judges between people on the Day of Resurrection over their disagreements.
The section asks whether God is not the wisest of judges; this ayah asks “who is better than God in judgment?” (ومن أحسن من الله حكما), contrasting God's judgment with the judgment of ignorance.
The section describes calling parties to God's ruling; this ayah says faith requires making the Messenger judge their dispute and then submitting without resistance to his decision.
The section defines ḥukm as restraint from injustice; this command explicitly joins judging among people to justice (أن تحكموا بالعدل), giving that definition a public practice.

The command to judge by what God revealed and not follow people's desires (ولا تتبع أهواءهم) shows judgment restraining partiality; the section's ḥ-k-m image moves from holding back harm to deciding justly.
“Judgment belongs only to God” (إن الحكم إلا لله), who tells the truth and is the best divider, closely matches the section's account of ḥukm as God's just decision.
The question “shall I seek another judge besides God?” (أفغير الله أبتغي حكما) names the same divine adjudication that the section finds in al-ḥākimīn.
After people disputed over the Sabbath, the ayah says their Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection; it joins the section's dispute, dīn-day judgment, and return to God.

After the Children of Israel differed despite receiving knowledge, their Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection; this is a concrete instance of the section's promised settling of disagreements.
The section says a party can be called to God's judgment; here people turn away when called to God and the Messenger “to judge between them” (ليحكم بينهم), showing refusal of that call.
Following the refusal in 24:48, this ayah says they come readily if the right is on their side; it identifies self-interest as the boundary that makes their response to judgment unreliable.
The next ayah asks whether their hearts are sick or they doubt, then calls them wrongdoers; it gives the refusal in 24:48 a moral diagnosis rather than treating it as a neutral disagreement.
The section's call to God's judgment is answered here by believers who say “we hear and obey” when called to be judged; it supplies the receptive stance opposite 24:48.

This ayah says family ties and children will not avail on the Day of Resurrection and that God will decide between people; it recalls Noah's appeal for his son while placing kinship under final judgment.
After rival scriptural communities dispute, the ayah says God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection; it is a direct instance of the judgment over disagreement named in the section.
The Prophet prays “My Lord, judge with truth” (رب احكم بالحق); the section's ḥukm as a just decision is here voiced as a plea amid accusations.
David is commanded to judge between people with truth and not follow desire; the section's bridle image of restraint and its definition of ḥukm as preventing injustice meet in this warning.

The next ayah after 6:57 says that if what the opponents hasten were with the Prophet, the matter between them would already be decided; it continues the passage's boundary between God's judgment and human demands for it.
The passage says God has no partner in His judgment (ولا يشرك في حكمه أحدا); this states the boundary implicit in the section's claim that Allah alone is the wisest Judge.
God “judges with truth” (يقضي بالحق), while those invoked besides Him cannot judge anything; the contrast gives force to the section's identification of Allah as al-ḥākim.
The ayah says judgment belongs to God and people return to Him (له الحكم وإليه ترجعون), closely joining the section's return and final authority.

After saying everything perishes except God's face, the ayah says “His is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned” (له الحكم وإليه ترجعون); it joins return and judgment as in the section's reading of 95:5 and 95:8.
On that day each soul encounters what it did and people are returned to their true Master (وردوا إلى الله مولاهم الحق); this supplies a second scene of return to the owner who judges.
At death, a person pleads “My Lord, send me back” (رب ارجعون) to do good; the section's dictionary form aḥkamtu means “I returned him,” and this scene makes return a denied plea for another chance.
The next ayah denies the plea in 23:99 and places a barrier until resurrection; it makes the return in the section's dictionary gloss a boundary controlled by God.
The section explains dīn as judgment, accounting, and requital, then names this verse: God is “Master of the Day of dīn” (مالك يوم الدين), so the day belongs to the One who rules it.
The section cites the oath's answer “the dīn will surely occur” (وإن الدين لواقع); it asserts the certainty of the reckoning named in 95:7.
The section cites this question, “what will make you know what the Day of dīn is?” (وما أدراك ما يوم الدين); it opens the same reckoning day that 95:7 asks people not to deny.
This ayah repeats the question from 82:17; the repetition sustains the question before 82:19 answers that command on that day belongs to God.
The section cites this answer: on that day no soul controls anything for another, and command belongs to God (والأمر يومئذ لله); it clarifies the sovereignty in “Master of the Day of dīn.”

On the day people appear with nothing hidden, the question “whose is the kingdom today?” is answered “God's, the One, the Prevailing”; it develops the section's d-y-n branch of mastery and subjection.

“Today every soul is repaid for what it earned; no injustice today” (اليوم تجزى كل نفس بما كسبت لا ظلم اليوم) unpacks the section's dīn as accounting and requital, while echoing ḥukm's restraint from injustice.
At the judgment, no soul is wronged and each is repaid only for what it did; this gives the section's “accounting and requital” gloss of dīn a concrete rule.

The ayah says each soul is repaid for what it earned and no one is wronged; its pairing of recompense and justice makes explicit the relation between dīn and the section's anti-injustice definition of ḥukm.
The record is set, witnesses are brought, and judgment is made “with truth” (وقضي بينهم بالحق) with no one wronged; this stages the just judgment the section names.
On the day every soul comes arguing for itself and is fully repaid for its deeds without injustice; this makes the section's dīn as reckoning, judgment, and requital a scene.
People are gathered on a day of no doubt and every soul is paid in full for what it earned without injustice; it is a direct expansion of dīn as accounting and requital.
The day God gathers people is called the Day of Loss and Gain, when faith and deeds lead to forgiveness and a garden; it gives dīn's reckoning and return a concrete division of outcomes.
This ayah says people “deny the Day of dīn” (تكذبون بالدين), the precise denial questioned in 95:7.
After 82:9 names denial of the Day of dīn, this ayah introduces the appointed recorders; it shows that the denied day involves deeds being kept.
The next ayah describes those recorders as honorable scribes, specifying the accounting scene introduced after the denial in 82:9.
The final neighbor says the recorders know what people do; it makes the record in 82:10-11 relevant to the section's dīn as account.
This ayah identifies those who deny the Day of dīn (يكذبون بيوم الدين), a direct parallel to the challenge in 95:7.
The damned say they used to deny the Day of Requital (نكذب بيوم الدين); it shows what the section's question asks its hearer to face.
The surah opens by asking about one who denies al-dīn; the following treatment of pushing aside the orphan makes denial of requital visible in conduct.
The next ayah depicts the denier from 107:1 as one who repulses the orphan; it gives a concrete social consequence to denying the day of judgment.
The continuation condemns failure to urge feeding the poor; beside the denial in 107:1, it shows conduct that the section's final Judge will weigh.
People emerge in separate groups to see their deeds; this is a compact scene of the reckoning that the section calls dīn.
The section connects dīn with account and requital; here even an atom's weight of good is seen, giving a smallest measure to the judgment of deeds.
The matching statement that even an atom's weight of evil is seen supplies the other side of the reckoning and balances 99:7.
The image of weighed deeds makes judgment measurable: those whose scales are heavy reach a pleasing life, giving a concrete form to the section's accounting and requital.
This next ayah names the pleasing life of those with heavy scales in 101:6; it adds the reward side to the weighed judgment.
The matching case of light scales states the adverse boundary of the weighing in 101:6, a concrete reversal of favorable requital.
The next ayah calls the light-weigher's destination “Hāwiyah”; it specifies the adverse outcome of judgment in 101:8.
This question introduces the explanation of Hāwiyah after the light scales in 101:8-9; the judgment's destination is made explicit in its neighbor.
The answer names it a “blazing fire” (نار حامية), completing 101:10's account of the light-weigher's outcome.
The section's dictionary description of qiyāmah says creatures stand before the Living, Sustaining One; this ayah says people stand before the Lord of the worlds (لرب العالمين).
On the day the Spirit and angels stand in rows before the Most Merciful, no one speaks without permission; it gives bodily form to the qiyāmah scene in the section's q-w-m gloss.
God promises support to messengers and believers “on the day the witnesses stand” (يوم يقوم الأشهاد); the standing witnesses evoke the section's qiyāmah as a day of standing before judgment.
After the trumpet is blown a second time, people stand looking (قيام ينظرون); this depicts the rising and standing that the section's qiyāmah gloss connects with the final court.
Faces are humbled before the Ever-Living Sustainer, and the wrongdoer fails; this joins the section's “standing before al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm” gloss to humility and the boundary against injustice.
The section's bridle image is restraint that corrects; here the one who fears standing before the Lord restrains the self from desire (ونهى النفس عن الهوى), an inward counterpart to that restraint.
The next ayah names Paradise as the abode of the person who restrained the self in 79:40; it supplies the outcome of restraint before judgment.
God fashions people and makes their forms beautiful, “then to Him is the destination” (وإليه المصير); this joins the best formation of 95:4 to the return in 95:5.
God creates, fashions, and proportionally forms the human being (خلقك فسواك فعدلك); this closely parallels 95:4's creation in the best taqwīm.
The next ayah says God composed the human being in whatever form He willed; it specifies the fashioned form in 82:7 and makes a direct parallel to 95:4's taqwīm.
The section points to the stages listed in Sūrat al-Qiyāmah; this preceding ayah begins that sequence with a drop of emitted fluid, before 75:38 says He created and proportioned.
This is the section's cited “He created and proportioned” (فخلق فسوى), a direct parallel to human creation in the best taqwīm in 95:4.
The next ayah says God made from the human being the two kinds, male and female; it continues the human-creation sequence around the section's cited 75:38.

The section explicitly compares the final question of Sūrat al-Qiyāmah: “Is not that One able to give life to the dead?” (أليس ذلك بقادر على أن يحيي الموتى). Its negative question expects assent to resurrection, as does 95:8's question expecting assent to God's judgment.
The human is created from a drop and proportioned (فقدره); this is a close formulation of the section's 95:4 image of the human made in best proportion.
After creation and proportioning in 80:19, this ayah says God made the way easy; it continues the sequence of what the Creator does for the human.
The human is then made to die and buried; this marks the low point between the fashioned human of the section and return to judgment.
The next ayah says that when God wills, He raises the human; after death in 80:21 this makes return from the grave part of the creation sequence.
The section reads 95:4-6 as human formation followed by a fall with believers excepted; “the human is in loss” (إن الإنسان لفي خسر) gives a close reversal of that elevated human image.

The exception of those who believe and do right, urge truth, and urge patience mirrors 95:6's exception of believers who do good from the lowly outcome; the two short surahs share a human-loss/faithful-exception pattern.
The negative question “Am I not your Lord?” (ألست بربكم) receives “Yes indeed” (قالوا بلى); the section explains that a question framed with negation expects the confirming answer balā.

When people stand before their Lord, they are asked “Is this not the truth?” and answer yes (قالوا بلى وربنا); this supplies the section's negative-question/affirmative-answer form in a judgment scene.
The section cites this negative question about the Creator's ability to make the dead live, answered “Yes” (بلى); like 95:8, the question's form puts the confirming answer in the hearer's mouth.
A negative question about the Creator's power to revive the dead is answered “Yes indeed” (بلى إنه على كل شيء قدير); this is another explicit resurrection form of the section's rhetorical question.

“Does He who created the heavens and earth not have power to create the like?” is a negative question whose context asserts the Creator's power; it parallels the form and creation-to-resurrection reasoning of the section's cited 75:40.

The section's named dictionary branch ḥikma defines wisdom as finding truth through knowledge and reason; this ayah names wisdom (الحكمة) as a gift from God and calls it abundant good, a direct use of that branch.
The section's source word ḥikma means wisdom; here the call to God's way is to be made “with wisdom” (بالحكمة), showing wisdom as a means of a sound, corrective address.

The ayah calls its preceding commands “part of the wisdom” (ذلك مما أوحى إليك ربك من الحكمة) and ends with worship of God alone; it meets the section's wisdom branch and its link between Allah and worship.
Jesus says he has brought wisdom (بالحكمة) and come to clarify some matters over which people differ; this joins the section's wisdom branch to its account of judgment settling dispute.

The section's dictionary branch defines ḥikma as right insight by knowledge and reason; this ayah names a far-reaching wisdom (حكمة بالغة) but says warnings do not benefit, showing wisdom's presence against refusal to heed.

The command to stand for justice even against oneself, parents, and kin checks partiality; it echoes the section's ḥukm as restraint from injustice and its image of holding back what would run unchecked.
The ayah warns that hatred must not carry people into injustice and commands justice; this is a specific moral restraint like the section's explanation of ḥukm as holding back wrongdoing.
The section's d-y-n branch includes mastering or subjugating someone; this challenge asks why, if people are not under God's power or recompense, they cannot return the departing soul (ترجعونها).
